title and abstract.summary: The study quantified the relative contribution of honeybees and wild bees to the pollination of apple orchards by examining three functional traits: body size, pollen load purity, and flower handling behavior. The measurements covered both honeybees and wild bees within the context of apple pollination.

introduction.summary: The study investigated functional traits of wild bees to predict seed set in apple orchards and then used these traits to estimate the relative pollination services provided by wild bees compared to honeybees across a regional scale in NY. The study measured the contribution of wild bees to seed set relative to honeybees in NY apple orchards.

methods.summary: The study measured the summed contribution to seed set of the entire wild bee community relative to that of the honeybee in NY apple orchards by using functional traits as a proxy for per-visit effectiveness and multiplying these trait values by the abundance of the bees. The study measured the relative pollinator contribution across apple orchards by analyzing functional traits of wild bees collected via standardized transects. The study measured the contribution of different bee species to apple seed set by analyzing the abundance of each species multiplied by the proportion of flower visits

results.summary: The study measured the abundance and foraging behavior of honeybees and wild bees in apple orchards, and modeled how these factors, along with flower handling behavior, relate to seed set at the orchard level. The study measured the contribution of wild bees and honeybees to seed set in orchards, and compared functional traits like pollen load purity and body size between the two groups.
